title: Solutions, Liquids and Solids
description: Why substances dissolve, how solutes change the properties of solvents, and how matter is organized in the condensed phases.
overview: In a gas the particles hardly interact. In liquids and solids they interact strongly, and every property from vapor pressure to melting point depends on the balance between attractions and thermal motion. The condensed phases are also where most chemistry happens: nearly all of biochemistry, analytical chemistry and synthesis takes place in solution.

This chapter starts with the liquid state and vapor pressure, then asks why solutes dissolve and how a dissolved solute changes the properties of the solvent (colligative properties). It then maps out phase diagrams and ends with the structure of crystalline solids.
objectives: Relate vapor pressure to temperature with the Clausius–Clapeyron equation.
Explain dissolution in terms of intermolecular forces, enthalpy and entropy, and apply Henry’s law.
Use Raoult’s law and colligative property equations, including the van ’t Hoff factor.
Read a phase diagram and identify triple and critical points.
Do heating-curve calculations that combine temperature changes and phase changes.
Describe common crystal structures, count atoms in a unit cell and compute density.

sections.title: Liquids and vapor pressure
body: Molecules in a liquid are close together and attract one another, but they are in constant motion, and a few at the surface have enough energy to escape. In a closed container, vaporization and condensation come to a dynamic equilibrium, and the pressure of the vapor is the **vapor pressure**. It depends only on the substance and the temperature. A liquid with high vapor pressure at room temperature is **volatile** (acetone, diethyl ether). A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the external pressure. The **normal boiling point** is the temperature at which the vapor pressure is 1 atm.
Vapor pressure rises steeply with temperature, because more molecules have enough energy to escape. The **Clausius–Clapeyron equation** describes this:
A plot of ln P against 1/T is a line with slope −ΔH_{vap}/R, so vapor pressure data give the enthalpy of vaporization.

example.title: Boiling point at reduced pressure
example.problem: Water has ΔH_{vap} = 40.7 kJ mol⁻¹ and boils at 373.15 K at 1.00 atm. At what temperature does it boil on a mountain where the pressure is 0.700 atm?

body: Two more properties follow from intermolecular forces. **Viscosity**, resistance to flow, is high when molecules are large or hydrogen-bonded (glycerol, honey). **Surface tension**, the energy needed to enlarge a surface, is high when attractions are strong. Water’s is 72 mN m⁻¹, which lets small insects walk on it. Water rises in a narrow glass tube (**capillary action**) because adhesion to the glass beats cohesion within the liquid.

check.a: Its vapor pressure equals the external pressure
wrong: Its molecules stop attracting each other
Its vapor pressure reaches 1 atm in any case

check.q: What does the slope of ln P vs 1/T equal?

sections.title: How substances dissolve
body: A **solution** forms when the solute’s particles disperse among the solvent’s. Three steps contribute to the energy: separating solute particles (costs energy), separating solvent particles (costs energy), and mixing them, so each solute particle is surrounded by solvent, a step called **solvation** (**hydration** in water), which releases energy. The enthalpy of solution is the sum. It can be positive or negative. A process with ΔH > 0 can still occur if the entropy gain from mixing is large enough.

The guideline **like dissolves like** summarizes the result: polar solvents dissolve polar and ionic solutes, because solute–solvent forces are comparable with solute–solute and solvent–solvent forces. Nonpolar solvents dissolve nonpolar solutes. Ethanol and water are **miscible** (soluble in all proportions) because both hydrogen bond. Oil and water are not, because the water–water hydrogen bonds would have to be broken for weak dispersion attractions in return. Salts dissolve in water through strong ion–dipole attraction.

A solution holding as much solute as it can at equilibrium is **saturated**, and its concentration is the solute’s solubility. A **supersaturated** solution holds more than the equilibrium amount. It is unstable and crystallizes if disturbed, as in a hand warmer made of sodium acetate. The solubility of most solids rises with temperature, but that of gases falls, which is why warm soda goes flat.
The solubility of a gas is proportional to its partial pressure above the solution:

k_{H} depends on the gas, the solvent and the temperature. For O₂ in water at 25 °C, k_{H} = 1.3 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ atm⁻¹, and for CO₂, 3.4 × 10⁻² mol L⁻¹ atm⁻¹. Opening a soda bottle drops the CO₂ pressure and the dissolved gas bubbles out; divers who surface too fast release dissolved nitrogen in their blood as bubbles (the bends).

example.title: Oxygen in water
example.problem: Air is 21% O₂. What is the concentration of dissolved O₂ in water in equilibrium with air at 1.00 atm and 25 °C?

solution.eq: c = (1.3 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ atm⁻¹)(0.21 atm) = 2.7 × 10⁻⁴ M  (about 8.7 mg/L)

solution: This dissolved oxygen is what fish breathe, and it falls as water warms.

check.q: Which would be most soluble in water?
Why does a carbonated drink fizz when opened?
check.a: The pressure of CO₂ drops, so its solubility falls
wrong: Opening the bottle heats the drink

sections.title: Vapor pressure of solutions
body: A dissolved solute occupies part of the surface and lowers the number of solvent molecules able to escape. **Raoult’s law** says that the vapor pressure of the solvent above an ideal solution is its pure-liquid vapor pressure times its mole fraction:

For a mixture of two volatile liquids each follows this law, and the total pressure is the sum. A solution is **ideal** if the A–B attractions equal the A–A and B–B ones, as for benzene and toluene. If A–B attractions are weaker, the vapor pressure is higher than predicted (positive deviation, as for ethanol and hexane). If stronger, it is lower (negative deviation, as for acetone and chloroform).

example.title: Lowering of vapor pressure
example.problem: Water at 25 °C has P° = 23.8 torr. What is the vapor pressure above a solution of 34.2 g sucrose (342 g mol⁻¹, nonvolatile) in 90.0 g of water?
solution: n(sucrose) = 0.100 mol; n(water) = 5.00 mol, so χ(water) = 5.00/5.10 = 0.980.

check.q: A solution has χ(solvent) = 0.80 and the pure solvent’s vapor pressure is 100 torr. The solution’s vapor pressure is…

sections.title: Colligative properties
body: A **colligative property** depends on the number of dissolved particles but not on their identity. Vapor pressure lowering is one. Three others follow from it.

Here m is molality, M is molarity, K_{b} and K_{f} are solvent constants (water: K_{b} = 0.512 and K_{f} = 1.86 °C kg mol⁻¹), and π is the **osmotic pressure**. The **van ’t Hoff factor** i is the number of particles each formula unit gives: 1 for sugar, nearly 2 for NaCl, nearly 3 for CaCl₂. Real values are slightly lower because ions pair at higher concentration.

list: **Boiling point elevation**: a nonvolatile solute lowers the vapor pressure, so the solution must be hotter to reach 1 atm.
**Freezing point depression**: a solute stays in the liquid and lowers its tendency to freeze. Antifreeze and road salt work this way.

**Osmosis** is the flow of solvent through a **semipermeable membrane** from the dilute side to the concentrated side. Osmotic pressure is the pressure needed to stop it. Cells swell in pure water and shrink in concentrated salt solution, which is why intravenous fluids are isotonic (0.9% NaCl).

example.title: Antifreeze
example.problem: What is the freezing point of a solution of 500.0 g ethylene glycol (62.07 g mol⁻¹, a nonelectrolyte) in 1.000 kg of water?

solution.eq: ΔT_{f} = (1.86)(8.055) = 15.0 °C,   so the solution freezes at −15.0 °C

example.title: Osmotic pressure
example.problem: Calculate the osmotic pressure of 0.100 M glucose at 25 °C.
solution: This would support a water column about 25 m high. Osmotic pressures are large even for dilute solutions, and measuring them is a good way to find the molar mass of a large molecule such as a protein.

example.title: Molar mass from freezing point
example.problem: Dissolving 2.50 g of an unknown nonelectrolyte in 50.0 g of benzene (K_{f} = 5.12 °C kg mol⁻¹) lowers the freezing point by 0.80 °C. Find the molar mass.

check.q: Which aqueous solution has the lowest freezing point?
check.why: i ≈ 3 for CaCl₂, so 0.30 mol of particles per kg.

check.a: From the dilute solution to the concentrated one
wrong: From the concentrated solution to the dilute one
Only if the solute can cross the membrane

sections.title: Phase diagrams and phase-change energetics
body: A **phase diagram** maps the state of a pure substance as a function of pressure and temperature. The curves are the conditions where two phases coexist at equilibrium.

body.caption: A generic phase diagram. The melting curve of water (dashed) slopes backward, because ice is less dense than liquid water.

list: The **triple point** is the one condition where solid, liquid and gas coexist. For water it is 0.01 °C and 611.7 Pa; for CO₂ it is −56.6 °C and 5.11 atm. Because CO₂’s triple-point pressure is above 1 atm, solid CO₂ sublimes at atmospheric pressure.

The liquid–gas curve ends at the **critical point** (water: 374 °C, 218 atm; CO₂: 31.0 °C, 73.8 atm). Beyond it the substance is a **supercritical fluid**, with no distinction between liquid and gas. Supercritical CO₂ dissolves nonpolar compounds and is used to decaffeinate coffee.
The melting curve of most substances leans to the right: pressure raises the melting point. For water it leans left, because the solid is less dense, so pressure favors the liquid.

body: Heating a substance at constant pressure gives a **heating curve** (see the heating curve of water in the chapter on matter and measurement). Where the temperature changes, the heat is q = m c ΔT, using the specific heat c of that phase. During a phase change the temperature is constant, and the heat is q = m ΔH, using the enthalpy of fusion (water: 334 J g⁻¹) or vaporization (2257 J g⁻¹).

example.title: From ice to steam
example.problem: How much heat converts 50.0 g of ice at −10.0 °C to steam at 110.0 °C? (c: ice 2.09, water 4.184, steam 2.01 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹.)
solution: The total is 152,520 J = 153 kJ. Vaporization alone is three quarters of it.

check.q: Above the critical point, a substance…
check.a: Is a supercritical fluid, with no distinct liquid and gas phases
wrong: Can be liquefied by raising the pressure

check.q: Why does dry ice sublime at 1 atm?
check.a: The triple-point pressure of CO₂ (5.11 atm) is above 1 atm
wrong: CO₂ has no liquid phase at any pressure
Dry ice is always above its critical temperature
Its molecules do not attract each other

sections.title: Crystalline solids
body: A **crystalline solid** has its particles arranged in a regular repeating pattern. An **amorphous solid** (glass, many plastics) has short-range order only. The smallest repeating unit of a crystal is its **unit cell**. By the kind of particles and the forces between them, crystals fall into four types:

Particles
Held by

Examples
rows: Hard, brittle, high m.p., conduct when molten
table.caption: Types of solids.

body: Graphite is a network solid of a different kind: layers of covalently bonded carbon atoms, held together by weak dispersion forces, so it is soft, slippery and conducts electricity along the layers.
Metals commonly pack as spheres. The number of nearest neighbors is the **coordination number**.

head: Structure
Atoms per cell
Coordination number
Packing efficiency
Edge a in terms of radius r
table.caption: Cubic cells. Hexagonal close-packed (hcp) also has coordination number 12 and 74% packing.

body: Atoms at a corner are shared by 8 cells (1/8 each), on an edge by 4 (1/4), on a face by 2 (1/2), and inside the cell not at all. Density follows from the cell: ρ = (number of atoms × molar mass) / (N_A × cell volume).

example.title: Density of copper
example.problem: Copper is face-centered cubic with edge a = 361.5 pm. Calculate its density.
solution: The measured value is 8.96 g cm⁻³.

body: In ionic crystals the larger ions, usually the anions, form a close-packed array and the smaller ions fill the holes between them. NaCl is an fcc lattice of Cl⁻ with Na⁺ in every octahedral hole (coordination 6:6, four formula units per cell). CsCl, with large Cs⁺, is simple cubic with 8:8 coordination.

Crystal structures are measured by **X-ray diffraction**. X-rays scattered from parallel planes spaced d apart reinforce when the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths: **Bragg’s law**, nλ = 2d sin θ.

check.q: How many atoms are in a face-centered cubic unit cell?
Diamond is very hard and has a very high melting point because…
check.a: It is a network of covalent bonds extending through the whole crystal
wrong: Its molecules attract by strong dispersion forces
It is held by metallic bonding

summary: Vapor pressure rises with temperature according to Clausius–Clapeyron: ln P vs 1/T has slope −ΔH_{vap}/R. A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the external pressure.
Like dissolves like. Dissolution depends on ΔH and entropy. Gas solubility follows Henry’s law, c = k_{H}P.
Raoult’s law: P_{A} = χ_{A}P°_{A}. Colligative properties depend on the particle count: ΔT_{b} = iK_{b}m, ΔT_{f} = iK_{f}m, π = iMRT.
Phase diagrams show the triple point, the critical point and the melting, vaporization and sublimation curves.
In heating-curve problems, use mcΔT within a phase and mΔH at a phase change.
Crystals are classified as ionic, metallic, molecular or covalent network. Cubic unit cells have 1 (sc), 2 (bcc) or 4 (fcc) atoms.

problems.q: Acetone has vapor pressure 185 torr at 20 °C and 400 torr at 40 °C. Estimate ΔH_{vap} and the normal boiling point.
A 0.0500 m aqueous solution of an ionic compound freezes at −0.274 °C. Estimate the van ’t Hoff factor and suggest a formula type.
problems.a: i ≈ 3: a salt such as CaCl₂ or Na₂SO₄ that yields three ions.

problems.q: A protein solution contains 4.00 g of protein per 100.0 mL and has an osmotic pressure of 8.5 torr at 25 °C. Find the molar mass.
Tungsten is bcc with edge a = 316.5 pm. Find its atomic radius and its density (M = 183.84 g/mol).
